Unloose
ŭn-lōōs´
v.t. (to untie, set free — rendering Greek luo, used of the latchet of a sandal)
From un- and loose, an intensive rather than a reversal. The Greek luo means simply to loosen; the office in view was the lowest household task, untying a master's sandal.

Biblical Definition

Unloose appears in the New Testament in one setting only: John the Baptist measuring himself against Christ. “There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose” (Mar 1:7); “one mightier than I cometh, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to unloose: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire” (Luk 3:16); “whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to unloose” (Joh 1:27). To untie a man's sandal was work so low that a Hebrew slave could not be required to do it; it was left to Gentile servants and to children. John, whom the Lord called the greatest born of women, says he is not fit for that office toward Christ. The comparison is not modesty but measurement: John baptizes with water, the One coming baptizes with the Holy Ghost and with fire. And John draws the only conclusion a true minister can draw: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (Joh 3:30). Mark adds stoop down, so the picture is complete — the greatest of the prophets, bending to the dust at another man's feet, and saying he is not worthy of the position.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines unloose as to loose; to untie; to set free from bonds or fastening; and notes that the prefix does not reverse but intensifies the sense of loosing.

expand to see more

UNLOO'SE, v.t. To loose; to untie; to unbind; to free from fastening.

UNLOO'SE, v.i. To fall in pieces; to lose all connection or union.

LATCH'ET, n. The string that fastens a shoe or sandal.

LOOSE, v.t. To untie or unbind; to free from any fastening; to release from restraint.

Key Scripture

Mark 1:7 — "And preached, saying, There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose."

Luke 3:16 — "John answered, saying unto them all, I indeed baptize you with water; but one mightier than I cometh, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to unloose: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire:"

John 1:27 — "He it is, who coming after me is preferred before me, whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to unloose."

John 3:30 — "He must increase, but I must decrease."

Modern Corruption

The minister is exalted into the place of the Master, and John's measurement of himself is treated as excessive humility rather than plain accuracy.

expand to see more

The whole ministerial disease of the age is answered by a sandal strap. John the Baptist drew crowds out of every city, baptized the multitudes, and was reckoned by the Lord Himself as the greatest born of women — and he said he was not worthy to perform the lowest household service for the One coming after him. This is not self-abasement for effect; it is an accurate reading of the distance between a herald and his King. Wherever a preacher's name, brand, or personality becomes the thing gathered around, that distance has been forgotten, and John's sentence stands as the correction.

Luke gives the ground of the comparison, and it is doctrinal rather than temperamental: I indeed baptize you with water; but… he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire. The minister administers a sign; Christ does the thing signified. No man can give the Spirit, regenerate a heart, or forgive a sin, and the office is honourable precisely because it points past itself. John 3:30 is therefore not a saying for particularly humble ministers but the rule of the office: He must increase, but I must decrease. A ministry not decreasing is in the wrong direction.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek luo (G3089), to loosen, untie — of the sandal latchet in Mark 1:7, Luke 3:16, John 1:27; himas (G2438), the thong or latchet itself.

expand to see more

Greek luo (G3089) — to loose, untie, dissolve; over forty times, including the loosing of Lazarus and of Satan.

Greek himas (G2438) — a strap or thong; the latchet of the sandal in all three Gospel sayings, and the scourging thongs of Acts 22:25.

Greek bastazo (G941) — to bear or carry; Matthew 3:11 has John unworthy to bear the shoes, the same office in another form.

Untying a sandal was the task of the lowest servant in a house, and Jewish teaching excused a Hebrew bondman from it.

Mark alone adds stoop down, completing the picture of the greatest prophet bending to the dust.

Usage

"“Not worthy to stoop down and unloose” — the lowest service in the house, and John says he is unfit for it."

"“I indeed baptize you with water… he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost” — sign and substance."

"“He must increase, but I must decrease” — the rule of every true ministry."
